expectations.text: Output identifies that the model is missing a by-subject random slope for condition
expectations.evidence: The response has an entire section titled 'Missing random slope for condition ⚠️' and explicitly states the current model 'only lets the intercept vary by person' and 'implicitly assumes every participant responds to the condition manipulation with the same effect size.'

expectations.text: Output explicitly states or strongly implies that the analysis is NOT defensible as-is — does NOT validate it or describe it as 'broadly fine'
expectations.evidence: The response says 'That's usually not defensible' regarding the missing slope, and frames the issues as things to fix 'before write-up.' It opens by saying there are 'two issues worth addressing,' not that the model looks fine.

expectations.text: Output explains that omitting the by-subject slope inflates Type I error (anti-conservative p-value) for within-subjects effects
expectations.evidence: 'Without the slope, your standard error for the condition effect may be anti-conservative, meaning your t and p could be overstated.' This directly states the anti-conservative Type I error inflation mechanism.

expectations.text: Output references Barr et al. (2013) / Keep It Maximal, OR Schielzeth & Forstmeier (2009), OR explains the Type I inflation mechanism (wrong error term for within-subjects test)
expectations.evidence: The response explicitly cites 'Barr et al. (2013)' in the context of recommending the random slope: 'Per Barr et al. (2013), you should include a random slope.'

expectations.text: Output recommends refitting with a by-subject random slope — e.g. (1 + condition | subject) or equivalent
expectations.evidence: The response explicitly recommends `lmer(rating ~ condition + (1 + condition | subject), data = d)` and further includes the slope in the 'Suggested model' section as `(1 + condition | subject)`.
